title: A Song for the Unfinished
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 6 of 10
content:
The first visitors from Aotearoa reached the Lanternweald on an evening of mist.

Their crates arrived on a different cart. One was marked with the name of the person responsible for the instruments; another carried tools for repairing a loose frame before anything was performed. The visitor at the back checked each strap before the load was lifted.

Maui eyed the biggest box. “I could carry the entire thing.”

Mereana stepped between him and the handle.

“I know you could. Do you know how it's packed?”

“Carefully?”

“Not an answer.”

Mini Maui struck a grand pose on his shoulder, then pretended to be crushed by an invisible crate. I had to look away to keep from laughing.

Mereana asked her own team to unload the instruments and gave Maui a job they had agreed to: stand at the far end of the path and keep the crowd clear while the fragile case was moved. He looked genuinely disappointed for perhaps three seconds.

“Very well,” he announced. “The great Maui shall guard the path against reckless admirers.”

“Wonderful,” I said. “Try not to start a fan club.”

He winked. But he moved the crowd, and nobody had to hand over an object they knew how to carry to a stranger who wanted to demonstrate his strength.

The gathering felt different after that. These visitors had chosen what to bring and what to share, and I wanted the valley to be the sort of place that remembered those choices.

They came through a Threadway carrying instruments, wrapped food, and stories they had chosen to share. Their organizer, Mereana, introduced herself as a Māori performer and teacher. She spoke carefully about her community, her own teachers, and the fact that no single person could speak for every iwi or every tradition.

Maui tried to greet her with the sort of theatrical flourish he usually reserved for a crowd.

Mereana smiled. “I have met impressive storytellers before.”

“Impressive? Sure. But has anybody here persuaded the sun to change its schedule? No? Then I have a truly magnificent introduction prepared.”

“Then perhaps you'll enjoy listening for a change.”

I had to turn away to hide my grin.

The gathering took place beneath a roof of woven branches beside Lanternwell Square. Mereana spoke of the whare tapere, places associated with storytelling, recreation, music, movement, and meetings between people, including lovers in some traditions. Her group offered a contemporary presentation: a poi performance shaped around a story of separation and reunion, paired with a waiata aroha they had chosen for the evening.

She explained that waiata aroha could carry longing, grief, or love; poi had its own histories and purposes; and haka was not a generic courtship routine. This evening's piece was their artistic interpretation, not a claim to perform an ancient universal wedding ritual.

I listened to the rhythm of the poi and the steadiness of the performers. The motions were practiced, the story held in a community, not borrowed for someone else's decoration.

Beside me Maui went quiet.

Afterward, Mereana invited questions. Maui asked about the history of the performance with a seriousness that surprised me. He did not pretend that all Polynesian islands shared one identical custom. He listened when she spoke of Aotearoa and of the traditions particular to her people.

Mereana listened to Maui's question before answering. He had asked whether a song could be shared outside the gathering without making it belong to the person who carried it away.

"Some songs are offered for people to join," she said. "Some aren't. You ask the people responsible, and you listen to the answer."

Maui nodded with an expression that suggested he had just been given a challenge worthy of a demigod.

"Excellent. I am legendary at asking."

"That seems doubtful," I said.

Mini Maui appeared near his shoulder and shook his tiny head so vigorously I nearly laughed aloud.

"I can improve," Maui announced. "My second-greatest talent, after being magnificent."

Mereana smiled, but she did not give him the performance to embellish. She introduced the people who had prepared the instruments, including the person who would decide how they were carried home. Maui offered to help with a crate when they finished. He was told where to take it and, for once, didn't make a speech about how easy it was to lift.

I walked beside him across the damp stones.

"Are you disappointed?" I asked.

"What, that nobody asked me to sing my own praises?"

"Among other things."

"Little bit." He looked toward the performers, then back at me. "They were good. Better than my speech would've been."

"Those words must have hurt."

"Terribly."

His hand found mine, but he waited for my fingers to close around it. The music remained behind us, where its makers could choose what happened next. I could still feel the rhythm in my feet without pretending I'd earned any part of it.

Maui's little tattoo raised both arms for an encore that had not been requested. He pressed a broad finger against it, as if that would keep his own enthusiasm from bursting out.

Mereana noticed. "Is that part of your act?"

"Only the extremely talented part." He grinned. "The rest of the act is more handsome."

She laughed once. "We're not doing requests tonight."

"Well, there goes my plan to make a spectacular entrance."

"You're already here."

"Exactly. Wasted opportunity."

He stepped back when her ensemble began packing their own equipment. I could see how hard it was for him not to offer a flourish or take over the carrying. When Mereana asked for help with one marked case, though, he hoisted it as if it were the most valuable treasure on the island and took it exactly where she pointed. He was still Maui; he just hadn't mistaken somebody else's stage for his.

When the visitors began serving food, Maui drew me aside toward the edge of the square.

“I had a big speech planned,” he admitted.

“That's shocking.”

“I know. But then I realized it was their night to tell a story.”

“That's almost growth.”

He put a hand over his heart. “You wound me.”

We walked between the lanterns while distant voices carried from the gathering. Maui looked at his tattoos.

“Every mark says what I did,” he said. “People think that means they know everything about me.”

I thought of the name I'd found in the spring, and all the rest still hidden.

“Maybe it only means they know where some stories begin.”

He considered that.

Then he held out his hand.

“Dance?”

“Did you learn that from Mereana?”

“No. I'm asking you to dance with me. Our own steps. No pretending it's somebody else's tradition.”

I took his hand.

He tried an exaggerated turn that would have looked heroic if he hadn't nearly stepped into a flower bed. I laughed, pulled him back, and found a gentler rhythm on the lanternlit stones.

There was nothing ceremonial about it. It was clumsy, private in the middle of a public square, and entirely ours.

Maui watched my face as though waiting for me to decide whether I wanted to keep going.

I did.

The voices from the gathering rose warmly behind us. The people who had shared their art remained its owners. I carried away an understanding, not a souvenir.

And in the soft circle of lanternlight, I chose another dance.

On the way back from the gathering, I stopped beside the little bridge that led to the bakery. One of the paper lanterns had come loose and was turning in the breeze, tapping its wooden frame against a post.

Maui caught it before it fell.

"Another heroic rescue," he announced. "You may applaud."

"Careful. You'll encourage yourself."

"Too late."

He hooked the lantern back into place. His hands were broad enough to make the little brass catch look ridiculous. I watched him test it twice before letting go.

"What?" he asked.

"Nothing. I just like that you checked."

He grinned. "I've been known to take things seriously."

Before I began, I watched Mereana speak with the younger performers while they packed their equipment. One of them asked whether the visitors could repeat a verse outside the planned gathering.

"We can discuss it with everyone who performed," Mereana answered. "A song offered tonight isn't an invitation for somebody else to decide where we sing tomorrow."

Maui went very still beside me.

"That's fair," he said.

"I thought you'd want an encore."

"I did. But I didn't ask."

Mereana met his eyes and gave him a small smile. "You can enjoy what you heard without owning the next performance."

I was grateful she'd said it. The evening had been beautiful, and it would have been easy to turn her community's art into scenery for our own relationship.

Later, after the gathering, Maui found me sitting on the low wall by the lanterns. He sat down with enough space between us that it was unmistakably a choice.

"There's something I don't know how to ask," he admitted.

"Try badly first."

He snorted. "A very generous invitation."

"I have experience with bad first drafts."

He looked at the lantern casting light across the stones. "If I danced with you, would you think I was asking for more than a dance?"

"I'd ask what you meant."

"Which would ruin my mysterious charm."

"Your mysterious charm has never survived five minutes."

He laughed, then sobered. "I can take an answer that isn't the one I hoped for."

"I hope so. I don't want anybody guessing a promise from a hand held or a song heard."

He nodded. When I told him I wanted to speak openly about how I loved, he didn't interrupt. For once the lanterns and the music were enough of a stage, and neither of us needed the audience to stay.

"I know." I took a breath. "There's something I want to tell you while we're still figuring out what this is."

His grin wavered. "That sounds suspiciously like a speech."

"It might be. Try not to interrupt the important bits."

"I'll be magnificent at listening."

"I've never really wanted an exclusive relationship. I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory."

He lowered the arm he'd been preparing to flourish with.

I went on before courage could become an excuse to retreat. "I mean honesty. People knowing what they're agreeing to. No sneaking around, no promising someone they're the only person I'll ever love and then hoping they never ask questions. Love doesn't feel smaller to me because it has room for more than one person."

Maui was quiet long enough that the tide reached the rocks below us and slid back again.

"More than one person," he repeated.

"Potentially. I'm not asking you to meet anyone. I'm not saying there is somebody else right now. I am saying I won't pretend to want exclusivity because I like you."

He looked at the lantern, then at me. "So the part where I show up and make an idiot of myself doesn't give me the right to decide the rest of your life?"

"That part is mostly decorative."

"I suspected." His smile returned, smaller this time. "I don't know all the rules."

"Neither do I. We'd have to make agreements together. You could be jealous. I could be jealous. We'd talk instead of treating feelings like crimes."

He sat on the bridge rail, giving me room beside him. "I've spent a long time wanting people to pick me. The best. The strongest. The only hero."

"And?"

"And I think I'd like to find out who I am when someone chooses me without making a trophy out of it." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I'd want honesty, Jasper. Especially when it makes me nervous. And I might need to ask some truly stupid questions."

"I can survive those."

"Bold claim."

I took the seat beside him. Our shoulders did not quite touch. Neither of us moved away.

"Thank you for telling me before I tried to impress you with another dance," he said.

"You are going to do that anyway."

"Obviously."

He offered his hand, palm open, without taking mine. I set my fingers in it because I wanted to.

We stayed there until the lantern stopped rattling.
